Networks (TCNs) hold great promise for handling time-series data. TCNs leverage a technique called time-dilated convolution that poses an optimization challenge which typically demands significant experimentation. We've developed a technique to automate the dilation optimization process by casting it as a weight-pruning operation along the time axis. Our method learns dilation factors concurrently with weights during training and achieves notable gains in model compactness and inference efficiency without compromising accuracy. It produces a range of highly optimal TCN variants from a single starting model, surpassing the performance of custom-designed networks in both efficiency and accuracy.

To address this, we developed an inequality that enables us to analyze the properties of the optimization landscape surrounding the solutions produced by an approximate message passing (AMP) algorithm. Specifically, we applied our inequality to demonstrate the local convexity of TAP free energy functions for a broad class of Hamiltonians, including those representing the Ising model, Boolean satisfiability problem, and certain continuous convex minimization problems. Furthermore, our results indicate that the AMP algorithm employs steps that are equivalent to minimizing the TAP free energy function within a certain locality. We also observed that for a certain class of Hamiltonians, the TAP free energy function exhibits multiple local minima, with distinct solutions separated by barriers. Notably, the AMP algorithm is known to converge to an overcomplete solution when initiated randomly; we found that this solution corresponds to a TAP equilibrium with zero spin constraints.

This theoretical framework includes Dull's and Giorgi's previous works as specific cases. The main idea involves using the Poincare map to analyze the dynamics within a surface of section and utilizing the first integral to transform this analysis into a two-dimensional problem. Then, according to Ghirlardi's results, the Poincare map can be represented as a expansion around the origin. To further investigate, Ghirlardi established the Lin-Liu-Cairlet theorem's application within this context, which enables linearization of the Poincare map near its fixed points. Combining these findings, the linearization theorem for smooth vector fields can be derived, considering assumptions of a full set of nearby first integrals and a specific nonresonance condition.

Literature can be broadly categorized into two main areas based on whether intermediate cues are employed: direct methods and two-stage pipelines.  The former includes pose-regression networks that directly estimate the pose from a single input image, while the latter utilizes intermediate cues such as object masks to facilitate the pose estimation process.  Despite their advantages, all existing methods suffer from certain limitations.  One-stage pose-regression networks often yield suboptimal results due to the complexity of real-world environments, whereas two-stage pipelines exhibit better performance but are cumbersome.  Furthermore, they frequently rely on synthetic data to train, which is not always feasible in practice.  To address these challenges, we introduce an internal-angle-based pose estimation framework known as iAPF, capable of estimating poses in a direct manner.  Unlike conventional networks that focus on projecting 3D keypoints to 2D image coordinates, iAPF computes the internal angles of 3D bounding boxes instead.  By doing so, it maps these angles to pixel coordinates in the form of 2D histograms.  Our proposed model leverages a Query-Key value triple (QKT) attention mechanism to process the histograms in a self-supervised manner.  iAPF, trained exclusively on image datasets, exhibits superior performance compared to existing one-stage pose-regression networks.

Bond-based Peridynamics has been a widely adopted approach for this purpose, though it lacks a clear connection to observed material behavior at the peridynamic scale. For a more nuanced understanding, Kelly-Omaiyekheri-Kim nonlocal damage peridynamic model has been developed to incorporate fracture within a peridynamic framework while adhering to thermodynamic principles. This paper delves into the detailed analysis of the kinetic and dissipation function of the Kelly-Omaiyekheri-Kim nonlocal damage peridynamic model, providing a comprehensive breakdown of the process. A deeper examination into the weak* continuity of the measure generated by the kinetic function is also conducted, ultimately leading to an exploration of the measure's weak* continuity under the condition that the initial data lies within a certain measure space. This line of inquiry has contributed to the derivation of an existence and uniqueness result for the boundary value problem.

We studied an array of Type IIB four-dimensional $\mathcal{N}=2$ effective field theories to uncover the range of universal symmetries potentially present and then investigated why they are avoided. Generalized $\theta$-terms emerge as crucial elements in these theories. These $\theta$-terms generate nonlinear connections between axion fields and quadratic gauge field strengths which can be used to break many universal symmetries. If we consider charged states as part of the scenario, additional universal symmetries may be destroyed, yet we found that the $\theta$-terms yield a Witten-like effect that indicates that the range of charged states is composed of an endlessly populated, lattice-like spectrum generated through the monodromy transformation, an element of the boundary near which the moduli space is established, and which defines the range of the effective theory.

scenarios where an adaptive adversary intentionally manipulates rewards and transition probabilities. The adversary's influence is confined to no more than an $\epsilon$ fraction of all training episodes. Notably, this attack model surpasses previously considered methods. We established a key finding that no reinforcement learning algorithm can discover an optimal policy better than $O(\epsilon)$ under these circumstances. Interestingly, we found that the natural policy gradient method can be robust when the corruption is bounded and is capable of discovering an $O(\sqrt{\epsilon})$-optimal policy. We developed a Filtered Policy Gradient (FPG) algorithm, capable of tolerating unbounded reward corruption, and achieved an $O(\epsilon^{1/4})$-optimal policy. The FPG algorithm represents a pioneering solution to robust reinforcement learning in scenarios with significant adversarial interference. Moreover, we verified the effectiveness of an FPG implementation utilizing a neural network on MuJoCo continuous control benchmarks. The results revealed that the FPG algorithm achieved only a small performance degradation, amounting to $O(\sqrt{\epsilon})$, when compared to standard policy gradient methods.

multi-phonon physics, is driving research and development for both fundamental understanding and applications in metrology and communication systems. Quantum acoustic resonators serve as the ideal testing ground for multi-phonon phenomena through a combination of theoretical and experimental studies. The specific system studied consists of a semiconductor quantum dot driven by a laser, coupled to an acoustic cavity, and has exhibited remarkable multi-phonon properties, albeit previously described with a simplistic two-level quantum dot model. However, by accounting for both bright and dark excitons within the quantum dot model, the complexity of this system can be better represented. The inclusion of dark excitons offers a particular advantage, given their inherently low decoherence rates as a result of lacking spontaneous photon emission. Consequently, researchers are now capable of achieving giant Rabi oscillations between a vacuum state and a dark exciton state accompanied by N-phonon bundles by adjusting the laser frequency with precision. Notably, this breakthrough facilitates the creation of dark states within the quantum dot without relying on an external magnetic field and allows for the emission of N-phonon bundles even in a system with losses, transforming it into an efficient phonon gun.

This model contains horizontal and vertical hopping terms and reveals two distinct non-equivalent Dirac cones within the first Brillouin zone along a high-symmetry path. yzed coherent states (SPCCSs) can be generated via quantum-optical catalysis using beam splitters or parametric amplifiers. These states occur when a coherent state and a single-photon state intersect and result in a reflected coherent state. We examine the process of generating SPCCSs using beam splitters and study the state's properties following reflection. Using this method, we find that the state's quadrature variance varies with reflection coefficient and can be minimized at specific angles, revealing an inherent duality in SPCCSs. This duality exhibits both bright and dark characteristics when analyzing the state's intensity. Additionally, our research demonstrates that SPCCSs exhibit non-local properties, resembling an entangled state when analyzed with the Hong-Ou-Mandel effect in mind. This provides a practical application for SPCCSs in simulating continuous-variable two-atom entanglement.

complex optimization challenges. Problems of control, estimation, and system design can be redefined as optimization problems subject to specific constraints. However, given the infinite dimensionality of these issues, it becomes necessary to employ numerical techniques to approximate a solution. We explore specific methods used in simultaneous direct approaches, specifically the transcription process. Our focus is on collocation, residual integration, and Runge-Kutta schemes, highlighting their applications to a case study related to the ventilator shortage during the COVID-19 pandemic. CT scans can be very difficult for humans or computer systems due to low contrast, the varying shape of the esophagus, and the presence of external objects such as feeding tubes. To compensate for these difficulties, doctors often rely on supplementary information from other imaging techniques, medical histories, and endoscopic findings. Acquiring and combining these sources of information is time-consuming and sometimes produces inconclusive results. In this study, we investigate the potential for a more streamlined clinical approach by presenting a limited set of text descriptions to a deep learning network designed to analyze CT scans automatically. These text descriptions highlight the difficulties of a clinical challenge known as indeterminate short segment esophageal lesions. To validate our approach, we compared results obtained by presenting the network with text descriptions against those from a previous study that did not include this supplementary information. The comparison showed a significant improvement when the network was provided with the additional text. Specifically, this improvement resulted in an average Dice coefficient increasing by 8.3%, a mean surface distance reduction of 3.5 mm, and a maximum surface distance reduction of 14.1 mm when the network was presented with the supplementary information.

One type of NER, nested NER, focuses on recognizing entities within other entities. Most existing nested NER studies apply linear models, which do not adequately capture the hierarchical nature of nested entities. This work overcomes this limitation by modeling nested entities as an integrated whole and proposing a new parsing algorithm to accurately identify all entities at once. Moreover, to address the lack of corpus-level information in NER, this study introduces features based on corpus statistics, including Point-wise Mutual Information, to enhance model performance and adaptability from sentence-level to corpus-level. Our experiments demonstrate state-of-the-art or near-state-of-the-art results on standard benchmarks and showcase significant improvement in domain adaptation through the proposed holistic modeling.

We look at curves defined by equations that are smooth, or at least have smooth properties in certain situations, over such modified fields. We express obstacles to counting these curves and their associated tangencies by altering the structure of these curves and their starting properties, focusing on edges and how they are counted. We show that by understanding how these curves and their starting properties are altered when changed in these specific ways, we can count these curves accurately. We use this to count these curves in different situations, over different modified fields, and when these curves are associated with other objects, such as points and curves in other spaces.

addressing the pervasive issue of data sparsity in recommender systems. Single-target and dual-target CDR approaches are often hindered by the limitations of requiring at least one well-supplied domain and over-reliance on domain-agnostic preferences, which is not reflectively realistic. To address these shortcomings, we introduce a novel framework called Multi-Sparse-Target Domain Recommendation Network (MSTDRN) to recommend items by simultaneously leveraging multiple inadequate domains with the aim of producing more authentic results. In MSTDRN, each domain is treated as a separate recommendation task characterized by its distinct sparsity level, and the network learns separate target preference representations for each domain simultaneously. A collaborative loss function guides the target representations to be adaptive, exchangeable, and domain-agnostic, while still maintaining fidelity to each individual domain. To facilitate MSTDRN's applicability, we introduce the Raw-Data Adaptive Sampling Strategy (RASS) to balance the imbalance present in real-world datasets by equally balancing the data across all involved domains. Experimental evaluations conducted on two diverse real-world datasets highlight MSTDRN's superiority over various state-of-the-art CDR methods.

various AI tasks, particularly in image recognition tasks, yet some challenges remain unresolved. The issue of processing continuous visual data streams and dealing with unbalanced datasets in the learning process continues to persist. Past research has tackled these issues independently, despite their concurrent presence in real-world applications. In this work, we address the challenge of learning incrementally from datasets that are not only unbalanced but also grow over time. We examine algorithms that rely on fixed deep neural network architectures, such as ResNets, for image recognition tasks. A review of current research reveals several criteria for evaluating learning algorithms, including their ability to adapt to new classes, retention of previously learned knowledge, and performance across datasets with balanced and unbalanced class distributions. We summarize existing approaches, categorizing them based on how they handle incremental learning, including algorithms that address single-case and general-purpose problems, as well as those tackling various real-world applications. Furthermore, we discuss the design choices underlying these approaches, including the architecture, loss function, weight update rules, and implementation details. Additionally, we present an exhaustive evaluation of 13 selected approaches in an effort to provide practical guidance for researchers and practitioners considering the use of deep neural network-based incremental learning for their own projects.

context, we explore a privacy-preserving approach called federated learning that enables several entities to train a robust machine learning model jointly, without exchanging sensitive information about their data. Based on how entities cooperate, FL can be categorized into two primary types: horizontal and vertical. In horizontal FL, participants with identical data characteristics collaborate to train a single model. On the other hand, in vertical FL, entities specialize in collecting distinct data characteristics and aim to construct a unified model jointly. Our review delves into the realm of vertical FL, focusing on scenarios where data characteristics differ substantially. Here, entities with unique data sets train individual models and then exchange them instead of sharing data. After discussing various FL protocols, such as TensorFlow Federated and PyFed, our analysis highlights the advantages of vertical FL over horizontal FL. Specifically, it offers greater flexibility in data collection practices and reduces data exchange requirements in exchange for increased computational demands and stricter consistency requirements. Moreover, vertical FL surpasses traditional learning approaches in regards to scalability, flexibility, and data privacy protection. Ultimately, joint learning methodologies like vertical FL strike a balance between data privacy and computational costs, positioning the field for future growth in machine learning powered by sensitive data.

Pyramid Networks (FPNs), frequently struggle with identifying large-scale objects due to an inherent drawback in the framework. This paper reexamines FPN within the context of detection systems and sheds light on its success through an optimization lens. It identifies that incorporating FPN results in distorted backpropagation pathways, limiting each backbone network level to focus on specific scale ranges. Consequently, two practical approaches are presented to empower each backbone level to consider all objects within the detection framework. Firstly, introducing auxiliary objectives facilitates direct propagation signals during training. Secondly, constructing the feature pyramid more reasonably can circumvent irrational backpropagation paths. Comprehensive experiments validate the analysis and demonstrate the efficacy of the proposed methods on the COCO benchmark, resulting in substantial improvements of over 2% across one-stage, two-stage, anchor-based, anchor-free, and transformer-based detectors.

crucial skill to understand real-world procedures, which often require grasping temporal common sense and incorporating various forms of information. Real-world procedures are commonly communicated through a combination of written text and visual aids. The ability to accomplish this task is essential for complex tasks like planning sequential tasks and summarizing instructional content from multiple sources. Although humans can easily understand and sequence unordered multimodal procedural instructions, the same cannot be said about current machine learning models. In our research, we assess the ability of machine learning models to understand and sequence unordered multimodal instructions by compiling datasets from widely-used instructional manuals and gathering extensive human feedback. Our findings show that these models not only struggle to accurately sequence events but also pick up on visual information that isn't present in the text. Interestingly, we discovered that what visual information these models pick up has nothing to do with the actual sequence of events. To improve the performance of these models, we developed an approach that involves training them to make predictions based on both text and visual information before getting feedback from human evaluators. Our results show that this method yields significant improvements, reaching human levels of performance for some tasks.

Researchers often study network immunization, but traditional approaches typically focus on broad measures, such as network criticality and component size. In contrast, this paper delves into a micro-level analysis, where the removal of individual nodes during an attack is examined in detail. Based on percolation theory, the authors analyze the effects of removing a single node that causes other nodes to disconnect from the main component. Specifically, this paper investigates the number of nodes that become disconnected from the main component as a result of removing one node. By applying this micro-level approach to a random attack on a Cayley tree network, the distribution of the resulting node removal sizes is derived.

biolabs and infectious-control hospitals must meet stringent safety standards set by bio-safety levels (BSLs) to prevent potentially deadly pathogens from escaping into the surrounding environment. These facilities maintain negative air pressure relative to the outside space by using specialized systems to contain the microbes. Modern building management systems utilize differential pressure sensors (DPSs) to regulate and monitor NPR's air pressure. Our research reveals a non-intrusive vulnerability in these systems, where an attacker can induce resonance in DPSs using malicious audio at their natural frequencies, causing the sensors to malfunction. Our findings show that the resonant frequencies of most DPSs fall within the range of human hearing. We have demonstrated that we can design music capable of generating these resonant frequencies and, in doing so, trigger a significant discrepancy in pressure readings. Our research shows that the malfunctions induced by this technique can fool the building management systems, potentially allowing pathogens to escape from NPRs. Furthermore, we demonstrate the practical applications of this technique by successfully breaching the security of an actual NPR. Lastly, we provide insights on how to improve the security of these systems, including the selection of DPSs with non-natural resonant frequencies or the implementation of anomaly-detection algorithms to identify potential malware.

Studies examining past experiences reveal a common issue with storage units - they frequently fail to take advantage of high-price signals during periods of low energy supply. This behavior has been often attributed to inaccurate forecasting or operational issues. However, our research suggests a more plausible explanation is rooted in risk-averse decision-making practices. Utilizing a stochastic self-scheduling approach and real data from the Australian electricity market, our findings show that risk-conscious storage units prioritize short-term cost savings by engaging in local price speculation, and tend to ignore opportunities in periods with unusual price fluctuations. This has significant policy implications, given the difficulty of detecting and managing storage units' risk aversion.

Moreover, densely generated proposals with adjacent semantics do not improve semantic distinctness. increasing interest in the Intelligent Reflecting Surface (IRS) technology. Comprised of passive reflective components that can modulate the characteristics of incoming waveforms, such as phase, amplitude, frequency, and polarization, an IRS offers a means to actively control the characteristics of wireless channels. Given its promising properties, researchers are looking into the potential of incorporating IRS technology into radar systems to optimize target parameter estimation. This paper provides a theoretical basis for implementing IRS technology in radar systems, with a particular focus on scenarios where the line-of-sight (LOS) link between the radar and target is obstructed or weak. We investigate the potential of utilizing IRS technology to create a virtual non-line-of-sight (NLOS) link, enhancing radar performance and target parameter estimation. Through numerical simulations and comparative analyses under both optimized and non-optimized scenarios, we demonstrate the effectiveness of the IRS-provided virtual link in target parameter estimation when the LOS link strength is lower than a relative strength of $~10^{-1}$ in comparison to the NLOS link.

A widely accepted evaluation standard in software testing is mutation analysis, assessing the ability to detect artificial flaws, and it encompasses a variety of measures that evaluate the ability to trigger and detect these flaws. However, mutation analysis is labor-intensive and expensive due to the need for mutation sourcing. a respiratory motion-compensated four-dimensional T2-weighted MRI sequence, which is crucial in radiology and radiotherapy treatments guided by MRI. Data acquisition is continuous via a spiral acquisition method with reordering of Cartesian sampling points (rCASPR) that ensures matching image contrast and sorts data into respiratory phases. Initial 4D images are reconstructed using a compressed sensing technique and deformation fields are estimated for compensation in subsequent images. Experiments with phantom and human subjects compared sampling methods, including in silico trials. Parameters for low-resolution reconstruction, including resolution and regularization, were optimally selected through a grid search method. Motion compensation in rCASPR was tested in eight subjects with results indicating better point-spread-function in rCASPR with little difference in contrast, thus making it feasible for direct application in radiology and radiotherapy treatments. Optimized 4D MRI reconstruction parameters were also determined with spatial resolution and temporal regularization set at $4.5mm^3$ and $10^{-4}$. A quantitative evaluation of image quality through the use of gradient entropy showed a score of 23.03 for motion-compensated rCASPR. Ultimately, this rCASPR-based method provides high-quality, free-breathing MRI images that minimize alterations in scan duration and image contrast, allowing direct application in radiology and radiotherapy treatments guided by MRI.

Sketch employs randomized linear measurements to map vectors into a lower-dimensional space, particularly effective at identifying the top elements (with the largest squared magnitude) of a given vector. However, the CountSketch sketch falls short in situations where subsequent vectors rely on feedback from previous inputs. Under such circumstances, the classic estimator can be compromised by a relatively low number of inferences, essentially making it vulnerable to manipulation. A more resilient estimator was proposed, which, albeit requiring quadratically more queries in proportion to the sketch size, significantly enhances the safety by a factor of k (with k being the number of key components) when compared to prior studies on CountSketch sketches.

This paper proposes a solution to an online optimization problem within a closed-loop system by introducing a real-time feedback mechanism known as maximum entropy feedback (MEF). or far-field detection, is a crucial capability for autonomous vehicles operating at highway speeds. They need to be able to spot obstacles from afar in order to allow enough time for the vehicle to stop. Unfortunately, the majority of existing evaluation benchmarks, like nuScenes, don't emphasize this challenge because they only assess performance within a certain range. There are a couple of key reasons for this. Firstly, annotating distant objects can be difficult because lidar sensors typically only return a limited number of data points at such great distances, making them ambiguous and hard to label accurately. Secondly, the conventional metric used to assess this task, centered around mean absolute percentage error, isn't well-suited for far-field object detection. As a result, there is a lack of clear guidelines on what a reasonably high scoring threshold should be for this task. As a result of these limitations, existing models may seem superior to historical ones simply due to their lower variance, rather than actual improvements. In order to address these challenges, we introduce a new evaluation benchmark called ThreeDSense. It differs from other benchmark datasets in a couple of key ways. Firstly, instead of focusing on the difficulty of annotating objects based on their density, it emphasizes the ambiguity of distant objects. Secondly, in order to mitigate the impact of loose scoring criteria, we propose a new evaluation strategy that breaks down object detection into two separate tasks - binary object presence and 3D bounding box size validation.

unclonable encryption, a unique feature in an encryption scheme where an adversary can't produce two encrypted versions of the same original message from a given ciphertext. Our research expands upon this concept, focusing on several aspects:

  - Flexibility in Usage: We've identified a significant drawback in the previous unclonable encryption constructions by Broadbent and Lord, as they either only guarantee single-use security in the plain model or security in the random oracle model. Our research presents two novel constructions for both public-key and private-key settings that maintain security even after repeated use and are founded on minimal assumptions.

  - Understanding Cloning Capacity: We've investigated the one-time secure construction proposed by Broadbent and Lord, specifically aiming to determine if achieving a nearly optimal $0.5^n$ success probability for cloning is attainable. Our findings generalize the construction based on various forms of monogamy of entanglement and present attacks against specific schemes with cloning probabilities reaching as high as $0.75^n$.

  - Applications to Copy Protection: We've discovered that strong forms of unclonable encryption can lead to enhanced security, specifically copy-protection for unlearnable functions. Our research paves the way for potential new constructions meeting these requirements, thereby expanding the realm of copy-protection methods.

To facilitate this process, WiFi fingerprinting, a technique where reference measurements with known locations are collected and analyzed, has become a standard approach in positioning methods and algorithms discussed in academic literature. However, measuring spatial distances between these collected data sets, also known as WiFi fingerprints, relies heavily on the choice of signal distance metric used to represent the similarity between them. Using simulations, researchers analyzed the characteristics of black hole X-ray binaries that could host a Dyson Sphere, discovering that such structures could be present in about 10% of these systems. With next-generation telescopes capable of detecting such relations, researchers could identify over 100 potential candidates for hosting a Dyson Sphere among the 4000+ known X-ray binaries, presenting a promising avenue for SETI initiatives.

Unlike unstructured environments where robots operate, structured domains like manipulation present a more promising context for imitation learning to excel. Current approaches for learning actions in this domain involve connecting the desired states to actions through a function, but these methods fail to consider the ordering of states that lead to the same action. To address this limitation, we introduce a new framework called the Action Graph, a structured representation of the domain where all possible states are arranged in an order, and the learning of actions is represented as a first-in-first-out queue. u-Goldstone (NG) theorem has been undertaken with an emphasis on its underlying mathematical structures drawn from Lie algebras, geometry, and number theory. The principles behind the anomalous NG theorem have been explored using both local Lie algebras and global Lie groups. In analyzing this phenomenon, a quasi-Lie algebra concept was introduced to bridge the gap between Lie algebras and their corresponding Lie groups, providing a framework for understanding the anomalous NG theorem. Certain key features of the NG theorem were found to retain their applicability even in situations broken by symmetry, known as anomalies. A comparative study of both sharp and soft anomalies was conducted. The formation of a kink in the anomalous NG theorem was recognized as a manifestation of a soft anomaly occurring due to a symmetry that is only asymptotically maintained. In contrast, a hard anomaly, also known as an infrared anomaly, arises from a symmetry that is asymptotically restored. An illustration of the anomalous NG theorem was provided using both bosonic and fermionic systems. An analysis of the anomalous NG theorem was performed in various contexts, including those involving symmetry breaking through a constant field and in systems characterized by a topological number. The results indicate that the anomalous NG theorem exhibits a direct relationship with the principles of a quasi-Lie algebra.

graphene holds significant promise, enabling the synthesis of highly lattice-mismatched materials and reducing waste from expensive substrate reuse. Nevertheless, concrete proof of a remote epitaxial process is yet to be found. Many instances are instead attributed to contaminants between graphene and the substrate, or alternative processes such as van der Waals epitaxy. This study discovered that when growing the Heusler compound GdPtSb on clean graphene substrates, it results in a unique 30 degree rotated superstructure, not explicable through other mechanisms. This rotation domain percentage significantly increases at lower growth temperatures. It's suggested that slower surface diffusion at lower temperatures favors the remote epitaxial process over faster surface diffusion at higher temperatures. Moreover, this study demonstrated that precise annealing of the graphene and consideration of film/substrate lattice mismatches are necessary for achieving epitaxial relationships with a range of Heusler compounds, including LaPtSb and GdAuGe. The distinctive 30 degree rotated superstructure offers a potential experimental signature for identifying remote epitaxy.

high energy radiation remains a mystery.  Hadronic radiation from the disks around supermassive black holes, formed when magnetic fields reconnect, could provide a potential explanation.  By applying this "MAD" model to the 15 most radiant galaxies, we found that it can account for gamma-rays in the energy band if the matter falling into the black hole occurs at a rate that's just a tiny fraction of its potential.  However, at higher accretion rates, absorption from the abundant low-energy photons hinders the gamma-rays, thwarting the MAD model's explanation.  Moreover, using an alternate approach to describe magnetic field interactions with electrons also led to the model's failure, revealing the significance of how electrons are energized.  The model was also applied to the central black hole at our galaxy, Sgr A*, and it failed to account for gamma-rays, leading to the inference that any gamma-rays emanating from this region would be insufficient to account for high energy cosmic radiation found on Earth.

Deep neural network-based classifiers have a common issue, however - they often provide predictions that seem excessively certain but do not reflect the true likelihood of classification accuracy. This limitation is attributed to the inherent closed-world nature of traditional softmax formulation. As cross-entropy loss encourages models to classify inputs into a fixed number of pre-defined categories, this can result in overly confident predictions that fail to capture true uncertainty. To address this shortcoming, a novel $K$+1-way softmax formulation is proposed. This approach involves introducing an extra dimension to account for uncertainty and proposes an innovative energy-based objective function to unify both classification tasks and uncertainty modeling. Furthermore, theoretical analysis reveals that optimizing this function effectively captures the marginal data distribution in the uncertainty dimension. Our experiments demonstrate that Energy-based Open-World Softmax, this proposed method, outperforms current best practices in enhancing confidence calibration.

This paper focuses on a model consisting of a two-level ecosystem where two species of predators, competing for a common prey, engage in explicit interference. The model is reworked to display a singular perturbation with rapid prey movement and slower predator movement, allowing for a regime close to the singular Hopf bifurcation to be analyzed. Near this point, the model exhibits chaotic, mixed-mode oscillations, consisting of long-lasting, concatenated periods of small and large amplitude movements. These eventually transition into the model's steady-state equilibrium. To determine the initiating factors behind a large amplitude oscillation in the mixed-mode orbit, the model is reduced to a suitable normal form, located at the singular Hopf point. The resulting normal form reveals a separating surface that distinguishes two forms of oscillations, and the occurrence of a large amplitude oscillation depends on whether the trajectory crosses over this boundary from the inside or outside. Conditions derived from the normal form can predict whether the model will enter another period of MMO behavior before reaching equilibrium. These conditions may serve as early warning indicators for a population shift in the ecosystem.

Typically, lower and intermediate mass stars retain their rapid rotation rates during their main sequence phase. However, once these stars expand into giants, we expect a faster core rotation rate compared to their outer layers. Contrary to these expectations, KIC 9267654's rotation speed is observed to be higher near its surface rather than at its core, which presents a challenge to angular momentum conservation principles. Lastly, we examined possible explanations for this unusual internal rotation profile, including the possibility of the star ingesting a giant planet or experiencing enhanced angular momentum redistribution through tidal inertial waves induced by a close-by brown dwarf or white dwarf.

Laser Interstitial Thermal Therapy (LITT) treats seizures caused by epilepsy in a specific brain area, the mesial temporal lobe. Evaluating the effectiveness of this treatment requires analyzing changes to the treated brain area after LITT, which can be achieved by examining changes in the type and activity of genes expressed in the area. Although this information can be obtained from preoperative and postoperative MRI scans, it is not sufficient on its own to accurately assess how well the treatment works. Additional genetic data, preferably noninvasive, is needed to accomplish this goal. Since EEG readings provide a window into the electrical activity of the brain and can be taken before and after LITT, we propose using machine learning to determine if these readings contain genetic information that could be used to better understand the effect of LITT on the brain. Our research demonstrates that certain features of the EEG readings are associated with the type of genes expressed in the brain area treated with LITT, and that further analysis of these features reveals patterns associated with the patient's seizure history. These patterns emerge when the patient has a seizure solely in the treated brain area, or in other brain areas as well. Additionally, we found that the amount of a particular substance, N-acetylaspartate, in the treated brain area is linked to the type of genes expressed in that area, and this substance has been previously associated with brain cells that produce myelin.

Due to its popularity, MongoDB has become a common choice for three-tier systems, web applications, and microservices, despite lacking built-in concurrency control. As a result, MongoDB's document-oriented data model and distributed architecture lead to increased risk of concurrency-related issues. 

While previous evaluations of MongoDB's concurrency behavior focused on specific use cases, this study aims to comprehensively assess the concurrent updates of MongoDB's document-oriented, distributed database across various scenarios. 

In our assessment, a systematic approach was employed to thoroughly examine the concurrent updates of MongoDB's distributed database. 

By developing a total of 129 test scenarios and running them on three-tier systems, web applications, and microservices built with MongoDB, this study successfully reproduced 17 risk scenarios associated with concurrency-related issues. 

The results indicate that MongoDB's concurrent update risks manifest in 17 distinct scenarios, and several preventive measures can mitigate the remaining risks with minimal performance impact. 

Furthermore, two risk scenarios proved irreparable and necessitated fundamental changes to MongoDB's API, resulting in only a 5% increase in overall performance costs after applying both fixes.

Menger developed an interest in the abstract concept of angle function, which he then generalized for use in metric and semi-metric spaces. Building upon this foundation, he presented two specific problems concerning the relationship between metric spaces and their associated angle functions. Over time, researchers focused on the one-dimensional aspect of angle functions and referred to them as metric functions. They ultimately made significant progress on one of Menger's initially posed problems. This paper aims to offer an in-depth exploration of the other problem first posed by Menger by introducing the notion of an order-preserving mapping called the interval function, which can be applied to the order-reversing mapping known as the bimetric function, both of which are interval-preserving mappings. Furthermore, this paper establishes that any interval-preserving mapping can be seen as a collection of metric functions and presents solutions to Menger's originally posed problems by providing examples using two-dimensional Euclidean spaces.

We analyzed real deer data to compare the accuracy of our method's estimates of population density and resource selection parameters compared to traditional methods. compatibility conditions, an operator with which it is invariant when applied to a given differential equation, is known as the direct problem. This process yields successive first-order operators for an n-dimensional manifold. The converse, an inverse problem, is to find the original differential operator when one of these compatibility operators is known. The compatibility operator can be parameterized by the original differential operator only if it defines a torsion-free differential module. The parametrization is minimal when this differential module has a vanishing differential rank. Notably, attempts to parameterize the Cauchy stress operator have been a subject of study for renowned scientists such as G.B. Airy, J.C. Maxwell, and A. Einstein. This work identifies a widespread misconception among them, mistakenly using the Cauchy stress operator and confounding it with its Laplacian component. As a result, the correct Einstein tensor was initially misinterpreted as the Cauchy stress operator.

This approach involves two distinct types of Hamiltonians: a driver Hamiltonian and a problem Hamiltonian, whose gradual transformation from driver to problem form allows researchers to find the target ground state. Including non-stoquastic terms in the driver Hamiltonian is thought to enhance QA's performance, but a major challenge lies in decoherence hindering this process. Surprisingly, we demonstrate that including anti-ferromagnetic interactions within the Hamiltonian results in catastrophic QA failure even with infinitely long annealing periods, a consequence stemming from block-diagonalization and symmetry analysis. Nevertheless, we find that adding anti-ferromagnetic interactions can be beneficial if QA is replaced by its quantum counterpart (QDA), and we show that this improvement arises due to the unique mixing of Hamiltonians during QDA, a benefit not attainable with QA. Our findings offer valuable insights into the design of quantum annealing experiments and suggest that multi-qubit systems should be studied further to understand the annealing process more comprehensively.

Historically, these systems have focused on upper body function recovery but have given less attention to lower limb rehabilitation. Studies utilizing non-invasive electroencephalography (EEG) have explored the restoration of walking ability in paraplegia but have limitations in decoding precise gait characteristics due to their low spatial resolution. Conversely, intracranial recordings (ICRs) offer higher resolution but are highly invasive, limiting their application as a BCI for gait restoration. This study introduces a high-resolution BCI system based on intracranial recordings for walking ability in paraplegia. Five participants with long-term spinal cord injuries underwent both EEG and ICR during treadmill walking tasks. Walking-related cortical activity was identified in both EEG and ICR data by comparing movement versus rest periods. Notably, the results showed high correlation coefficients between the features extracted from both EEG and ICR during the same walking sessions. Furthermore, the features obtained from EEG led to accurate classification of gait characteristics, including cognitive decisions to start and stop walking, as well as the speed of walking, as previously successfully achieved with ICR. These findings pave the way for the development of a hybrid BCI system combining the non-invasive EEG component with the high-resolution intracranial component, potentially enabling the restoration of walking ability in paraplegia without the need for invasive implants.

, like graph neural networks, have effectively tackled classification and link prediction tasks by capturing complex data representations. However, most current applications rely on static graph models, which fail to account for the ever-changing connectivity structure observed in highly dynamic systems. Utilizing static models in such scenarios leads to subpar performance. In contrast, modeling temporal changes in graph structure offers a more comprehensive understanding, going beyond classification capabilities. Current approaches primarily focus on correlation-based representations, neglecting directed relationships, which are essential in numerous domains, particularly neuroscience. Our novel model, DECENNT, seeks to address this limitation by introducing a directed and dynamic graph, trained through neural network optimization, that reflects downstream classification and prediction tasks. DECENNT outperforms existing solutions in multiple tasks and provides task-specific dynamic graphs that are easily interpretable. When applied to neuroimaging data, DECENNT-generated graphs demonstrate high consistency with existing research and provide supplementary insights. Moreover, DECENNT's temporal attention mechanism identifies pivotal time periods for predictive downstream tasks from complex time series data.

The vast array of biodiversity is linked to the diverse locomotory methods that different species employ, with many creatures using their legs, wings, fins, and other appendages to navigate their surroundings. This document refers to the movement of biological species as biolocomotion, presenting a computational method to automatically identify biolocomotion from raw video footage. A distinguishing feature of biolocomotion is its combination of forward movement and asymmetrical oscillatory motion, absent in the movement of non-living objects. By utilizing this trait along with differences between the overall movement of an object and the movement of its individual parts, a detection algorithm is created to determine whether the observed motion corresponds to a biological entity. Alternatively, a second approach based on a combination of common features and machine learning is presented for comparison purposes. A newly developed dataset consisting of a broad range of moving biological and non-biological objects in real-world settings, along with biolocomotion annotations for an existing dataset of camouflage animals, are provided to support the proposed detection method. Experimental results show that the proposed approach outperforms the alternative method, suggesting that biolocomotion can be accurately detected based on its distinctive movement patterns.

The test's asymptotic distribution is analyzed under various scenarios, including fixed and increasing network dimensions, null hypotheses, and specific alternative hypotheses. Key findings indicate that when model parameters are identifiable, the test's distribution converges to the chi-square and noncentral chi-square forms. Notably, the results are robust to parameters at their space boundaries. For non-identifiable parameters, an alternative test has been proposed, along with an established asymptotic distribution for a fixed network dimension. Given the challenges of tabulating test critical values, an empirical approach is implemented for p-value calculation. This includes the use of feasible bounds and bootstrap approximations. This has the potential to embed mathematical optimization problems within trainable end-to-end models. By providing an alternative expression for computing derivatives, this differentiability enables significant reductions in memory requirements, obviating the need for unrolling optimization procedures during backward passes. However, this typically requires the computationally expensive inversion of large Hessian matrices. In this research, we examine two specific applications - robust vector pooling and optimal transport - to illustrate how problem structures can be leveraged to achieve more efficient computations during backward passes, reducing both memory and processing requirements. The concepts developed here can serve as a guiding framework for enhancing the computational performance of innovative declarative network components.

Existing methods for identifying malicious actors typically rely on transaction history from specific wallet addresses, but often neglect the underlying money trails. These correlations reveal insights into the nature of hadron formation and the interaction between hadrons and the medium created in heavy-ion collisions. Hadron distributions in $d$$+$Au and $p$$+$$p$ collisions follow expected patterns, with hadrons moving in the same direction due to the momentum shared between them. Additionally, hadrons emitted in the same direction in Au$+$Au collisions exhibit a greater momentum difference compared to their counterparts in $p$$+$$p$ collisions. This increased momentum difference in the same direction could be a sign of hadrons interacting with a quark gluon plasma or medium.

working has been on the rise, leading many to adapt Agile methodologies such as Scrum to cope with distributed teams. However, the global shift to fully remote working brought about by the COVID-19 pandemic was a unprecedented phenomenon. This research involves a two-phase, multi-method approach. Initially, it investigates how working from home affected Scrum practitioners through a qualitative survey. Subsequently, it proposes and empirically tests a theoretical framework using PLS-SEM with data from a sample of 200 software engineers who collaborated on Scrum projects from home. Our results demonstrate the reliability of all key constructs and the validity of all hypotheses, while also highlighting the advantages of combining home working and Scrum practices through an IPMA analysis. Notably, supporting employees' inherent needs for autonomy, competence, and relatedness is crucial in the remote working context. Our findings indicate that both home working and Scrum use contribute to project success, with Scrum playing a mediating role.

is the uncertainty that arises when robots navigate deformable terrain. This challenge stems from the unpredictable behavior of terrain dynamics caused by ground deformation. Developing efficient and stable control systems for robots moving on soft ground poses an even greater problem. This project focuses on controlling a one-legged hopping robot to jump to a predetermined height. Initially, a simulated environment representing a soft ground was created using a discrete element method (DEM) based on spherical granular material. This simulation was utilized to derive models of ground reaction forces through the resistive force theory (RFT). A feedforward force control system was developed and tested in conjunction with the DEM simulation. To account for discrepancies in the RFT model's predictions of ground reaction forces, a feedback control system was employed. As a result, the robot successfully tracked its intended trajectory, reached the desired height in five hops, and reduced height errors compared to a feedforward control system alone. Furthermore, by increasing the robot's foot area from 1cm^2 to 49cm^2, the feedback controller demonstrated its ability to adapt to changing ground reaction forces, even when the model's predictions became less accurate.

considering negation, a fundamental aspect of all human languages. Despite being present in every language, negation poses significant challenges to current natural language processing systems. To accelerate the advancement of models capable of accurately processing negation, we introduce CONDAQA, a pioneering English reading comprehension dataset. It demands that models infer the implications of negated statements within passages, collected from a diverse set of paragraphs featuring varied negation cues. Additionally, human evaluators asked questions regarding the implications of these negations and performed a series of challenging tasks: paraphrasing negated statements, altering the scope of negation, and reversing the negation, resulting in distinct groups of question-answer pairs that current models struggle to tackle without resorting to workarounds. Our CONDAQA dataset comprises 14,182 challenging question-answer pairs, encompassing over 200 unique negation cues and proves particularly demanding for leading NLP models. Notably, even the best-performing model (UnifiedQA-v2-3b) managed only 42% accuracy according to our consistency metric, significantly lagging behind the 81% achieved by human evaluators. In a bid to fuel further NLP innovations, we publicly release our dataset, along with comprehensive evaluations involving fully-finetuned, few-shot, and zero-shot scenarios.

interlayer tunneling models were the prominent theoretical concepts to describe cuprate superconductors by connecting CuO planes through Josephson coupling. Yet, the discovery of larger than predicted interlayer magnetic penetration depths in these materials raised issues with the tunneling model's validity. The emergence of planar stripes and charge domains enabled alternative Josephson coupling theories. Our study finds the average intralayer interaction to be greater than interlayer coupling and comparable to condensation energy, ultimately yielding long-range phase order-driven superconductivity. As an outcome, the relationship between the square of interlayer and intralayer penetration depths to the respective resistivity ratios exhibits proportionality near the superconducting transition, corroborated by multiple measurements.

Since neutron stars are directly related to their progenitor stars, a study into the effects of dense matter uncertainty is also a investigation into uncertainty in neutron star progenitor masses.  By utilizing a set of 200 diverse relativistic EoS models derived from simulations of relativistic many-body theories, we calculated a range of birth masses for non-rotating neutron stars of 1.35 solar masses.  This calculation involved collapsing a typical 5-solar-mass progenitor star through its own gravity, and then analyzing the resulting neutron star.  The birth mass range for neutron stars of 1.35 solar mass mass is 5.03+-0.26, +/-0.26 (statistical)/ +/-0.53 (systematic) solar masses.  This large uncertainty in birth mass (approximately 17%) is primarily due to the diverse compositions of dense matter found in the various EoS models, which further highlights the need for more precise stellar progenitor information through the use of multi-dimensional simulations.

two-dimensional solitons, like those for Bose-Einstein condensates described by the Gross-Pitaevskii equations, have the property of Galilean invariance. This allows for solitons to be moved from a stationary state by incorporating invariance. Researchers face a challenge in finding models capable of exhibiting stable, self-accelerating motion of solitons. Self-accelerating modes are well-documented in linear systems in the form of Airy waves, but these waves exhibit poor localization. This concise analysis presents a pair of two-component Bose-Einstein condensate models which can accurately predict the existence of self-accelerating solitons. One such model, featuring interacting 1D solitons, involves the interaction between component BE condensates with negative mass and zero chemical potential, whereas the second model, also concerning two-dimensional systems, involves the interaction between dark-light solitons within a BE condensate. Additionally, this analysis suggests that all self-accelerating modes have a common trait - they can only be generated when a certain threshold is surpassed, and it is also claimed that this Bose-Einstein condensate system possesses the highest degree of Galilean invariance when two-dimensional component BE condensates are perfectly balanced.

a model from distributed data on a graph is a challenging task, especially when it comes to Federated Learning. A significant obstacle in this process is the substantial communication required between nodes and the server. A common strategy used to address this issue involves each node making several local model updates before sharing the updated model with the server. Although this method reduces communication costs, it introduces statistical disparities among the nodes' data sets, leading to slower model convergence and biases. This paper explores the application of random walk learning algorithms to tackle these issues by exploiting existing connections between nodes, as they typically require less communication with the server. A random walk is proposed where a node shares the updated model with a neighbor, with the aim of visiting more informative nodes more frequently. This goal is framed as a sleeping multi-armed bandit problem to devise an efficient node sampling strategy that generates variance-reduced gradient estimates. A novel adaptive random walk learning algorithm is introduced and proven to converge theoretically. Moreover, our results demonstrate its superior performance compared to other random walk algorithms.

This work delves into finding Generalized Maximum Likelihood Estimators (GMLE) to solve this estimation problem. Key properties and GMLE representations are explored and we discuss how a previous result from Kiefer and Wolfowitz (1956) can be applied to this context, including the scenario where the parameters $\theta_1,...,\theta_n$ are treated as fixed constants. Furthermore, we discuss estimators for $\eta_G$ and provide a representation that involves the empirical distribution function, which leads to consistency and central limit theorem results. GMLE is particularly useful in estimating parameters for mixture models and extensions of Dirichlet processes, and notable examples include estimating the posterior mean of parameters in Bayesian models and predicting regression coefficients in extensions of autoregressive models.

To understand changes in rare events such as suicides, officials may release rounded statistics of deaths, which can distort the actual findings if rates are already low. Our analysis reveals that in certain cases such as the Poisson distribution, rounding has a noticeable effect on the actual values, whereas in binomial distributions, the impact diminishes as the number of trials increases. The problem of pinpointing which training examples are responsible for a trained model's inaccuracies or biases has gained significant attention over the past decade. The computation of the Shapley value for training examples with respect to validation accuracy and model fairness has become a popular framework for tackling this issue. Although recent studies have made progress in computing the Shapley value for a single machine learning model in isolation, they fail to account for a comprehensive machine learning pipeline consisting of data preprocessing, feature extraction, and model training. To bridge this gap, a new system, DataScope, has been designed to efficiently compute the Shapley value for training examples within an end-to-end machine learning pipeline, particularly for a type of pipeline referred to as a canonical pipeline, characterized by a supervised learning model and a robust data preprocessing process. DataScope's innovative approach enables the computation of the Shapley value for a wide range of canonical pipeline configurations, including those involving dimensionality reduction techniques such as PCA and t-SNE, as well as robust data preprocessing methods like imputation and encoding. Furthermore, DataScope's design includes an user-friendly interface that facilitates the troubleshooting of training data quality issues within a comprehensive machine learning pipeline.

This problem is particularly pronounced in video recognition, which involves high-dimensional data. In an attempt to overcome these constraints and unlock the full potential of LSTMs, this paper proposes an integrated design of algorithms and hardware to achieve high-performance, energy-efficient LSTM networks. At the algorithmic level, a new LSTM structure called FDHT-LSTM is developed, which significantly reduces model complexity without sacrificing accuracy. In addition to this optimized algorithm, a customized hardware platform is also designed to efficiently execute the FDHT-LSTM model by incorporating a sophisticated memory access scheme that minimizes data conflicts and allows for real-time matrix transformations. Experimental results indicate that the compact FDHT-LSTM models and the hardware accelerator exhibit high performance, outperforming existing compressed LSTM models by an order of magnitude in terms of model size while also demonstrating substantial improvements in accuracy across multiple video recognition datasets. Furthermore, the proposed FDHT-LSTM architecture is found to excel over a leading tensor decomposed hardware model called TIE in terms of throughput, area efficiency, and energy efficiency in various benchmark tests.

As a means of enhancing NLP data efficiency, data augmentation techniques have been investigated in recent years. A systematic examination of data augmentation in NLP under low-labeled data settings has been lacking until now, resulting in difficulty in comprehending the efficacy of diverse methods in various contexts. single-phase Darcy flow within a fractured porous media, incorporating two types of fractures. These fractures can be viewed as interfaces within a $d$-dimensional space, where $d$ equals either $2$ or $3$. A significant distinction is drawn between fractures that function as Dirichlet boundaries and those that serve as Neumann boundaries. Our proposed method involves splitting the fracture interfaces into edges belonging to either type. To solve the problem, we employ a two-step approach for constructing the semilinear equation's solution. Initially, we find a hypothetical "pressure potential" function, which enables us to determine the actual Darcy pressure. A key aspect of our method is the development of local nonconformity techniques for both construction and reconstruction purposes. These methods involve establishing nonconformity mortar elements, as well as a novel approach to handling the Neumann-type fractures. We provide error estimates for both the "pressure potential" and the actual Darcy pressure. Furthermore, we demonstrate the feasibility of our approach through numerical experiments.

cognitive science, where Bayes factors can compare and contrast competing theories by assessing their consistency with available data. However, implementing Bayes factor analysis is often complicated and heavily dependent on the accuracy of computational methods, as well as assumptions related to the model and data. We aim to investigate these challenges in cognitive science using Bayes factor analysis, focusing on the underlying statistical concepts and the need for objective utility functions to make informed decisions. We explore various issues with Bayes factor estimates, including their tendency to err and the reliability of bridge sampling, especially when analyzing complex scenarios. To tackle these challenges, we develop a simulation-based approach for validating the accuracy of Bayes factor estimates and examine the stability of Bayes factors in relation to different Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) draws. We also investigate the variability of Bayes factor estimates and the effectiveness of utility functions in making informed decisions. To facilitate the assessment of Bayes factor reliability, we outline a step-by-step workflow that researchers can use to evaluate the performance of Bayes factor analysis for their individual studies, including an illustrative example from the cognitive sciences. We anticipate that this research will contribute to the development of a robust methodology for evaluating scientific hypotheses based on Bayes factor analysis, along with reproducible code available online.

Researchers have lately shown substantial interest in explosive synchronization phenomena which enable sudden shifts between these states due to their rapid and drastic nature. Although previous studies have highlighted key attributes of complex systems capable of explosive synchronization, these analyses were primarily undertaken on a case-by-case basis. This work establishes an exact standard for identifying explosive synchronization within coupled oscillator ensembles by determining the critical relationship between disorder in their internal workings and structure. This breakthrough brings us closer to understanding the intricacies of complex systems responsible for abrupt transitions and dual stability in both living organisms and man-made systems.

Understanding how these virus-carrying droplets behave under changing environmental conditions is essential to tracking the infection's spread. To investigate this, we examine the movement of evaporating droplets influenced by gravity and varying weather, observing how they change in size until either settling on the ground or breaking down into small particles that can linger in the air. The research into droplet behavior can inform strategies for preventing the spread of the virus, and the underlying principles can be applied to similar respiratory viruses.

This difficulty arises from not only the random fluctuations inherent to noisy data but also limitations imposed by data quantity, model specifications, hyperparameters, optimization techniques, sampling, and overfitting. We reevaluate how much is currently known about individual components of this matrix, making no assumption about its unitarity. We establish two fundamental sets of experimental limitations - direct plus inherent constraints, and indirect ones. We examine the effects of each set on the neutrino disk area, which represents the extent of neutrino data already analyzed. We conclude that existing constraints are sufficiently strict to require new neutrino experiments to consider the non-unitarity of the neutrino matrix. Our focus on FedSA originates from the common obstacle encountered when attempting to exchange model data. Researchers and organizations typically invest significant resources in developing powerful neural networks but, due to data protection, cybersecurity concerns, or ownership restrictions, they cannot freely share their trained models, despite wishing to contribute to the community. To address this challenge, we propose the FedSA approach, taking it one step further as it enables a student to excel in a different task than the teachers from which it draws information. To effectively handle FedSA, we implemented a custom technique where the student model is created using a saliency-based method that allows it to selectively engage with relevant teachers and incorporate their unique features. To validate the FedSA model, we conducted comprehensive experiments under both single-task and multi-task settings, and our findings show that FedSA successfully combines knowledge from disparate sources, outperforming comparable centralized models.

grid cells within the medial entorhinal cortex of rats was first identified. rotation undergoes significant changes, following distinct phases. Upon reaching the zero-age main sequence, its overall rotational velocity slows down, adhering to Skumanich's law and making gyrochronology possible. As they age, some solar-type stars may eventually transition out of this braking phase. Additionally, 3D simulations of these stars have identified various differential rotation patterns, characterized by the Rossby number. Specifically, anti-solar differential rotation, characterized by rapid polar rotation and slow equatorial rotation, can occur in high-Rossby-number, slowly rotating stars. If this regime emerges during the main sequence and persists in slow rotators, it may impact poloidal magnetic field generation through the $\alpha$-$\Omega$ dynamo process, potentially reversing the polarity of the magnetic field. As such stars transition to the giant branch, their potential anti-solar differential rotation may facilitate magnetic activity in low-mass giants like $\epsilon$ Eridani.

Investigating whether the quantum null energy condition limits irreversible entropy generation during quenching driven by an influx of energy and momentum from an infinite, memoryless bath within two-dimensional holographic theories, our research finds that an increase in both entropy and temperature, as required by the classical Clausius inequality, is necessary to prevent a violation of the quantum null energy condition, specifically in quenching transitions that result in changes in thermal states dual to Banados-Teitelboim-Zanelli geometries. Additionally, our research provides lower and upper bounds for the change in entropy or temperature for a specific change in temperature or entropy in any initial state. Our study demonstrates that the entanglement entropy within a region of a specific length, $l$, eventually reaches a steady-state within a time frame of $l/2$ with an exponential decay rate of $3/2$, and that the coefficient for the quadratic growth of entanglement in time can be found for any $l$, and that the asymptotic rate of growth for a semi-infinite interval is directly proportional to the difference of the entropy densities of the initial and final states,

's atmosphere, examining how its composition has been shaped by interior-exterior interactions over time. Despite significant ongoing research, key aspects of the atmosphere's formation and current state remain unclear and require interdisciplinary analysis. We examine various processes that have influenced the atmosphere's evolution, starting with volatile sources and examining interactions from the planet's core to its upper atmosphere, as well as atmospheric escape mechanisms. We also delve into the complex historical events that have contributed to the atmosphere's evolution, including the effects of impacts, magnetic field generation, and geochemical and geodynamic feedback cycles. We then outline plausible pathways for the planet's evolution, ranging from its accretion phase to its present state, using modeling and observations. These scenarios include atmospheric escape during the magma ocean phase, prolonged surface liquid water that eventually gave way to a runaway greenhouse phase, and water retained within the planet due to inefficient outgassing, leading to hydrogen entrapment in the core and mantle oxidation. We review the existing evidence and discuss the need for future research, as well as potential observations and missions required to better understand Venus's complex interior, surface, and atmospheric interactions and how they have influenced the planet's evolution and future.

GPU and TPU advancements, have significantly scaled tensor network algorithms for complex quantum simulation and machine learning applications. The quantum-inspired nature of these algorithms makes them mappable to parametrized quantum circuits (PQCs), which is now fueling proposals for leveraging near-term quantum devices to enhance algorithm performance. Furthermore, joint quantum-classical frameworks can exploit the unique strengths of TNs and PQC models. Notably, TNs provide a precise representation of classical statistical systems, whereas PQC serve as versatile approximators. To harness their combined potential, we propose TN-PQC hybrids through the use of the Jordan-Wigner transformation and a novel sampling technique that outperforms full-circuit simulations for certain chemical dynamics. Our approach involves developing a classical chemical dynamics simulation using the Jordan-Wigner transformed fermionic TNs and subsequently mapping this simulation to a quantum circuit, which can then be used to simulate the chemical reaction rates. We compare our proposed hybrid approach with the full-circuit simulation method and found that it yields a 6x improvement in TN decomposition accuracy at a 10x reduction in computational cost, achieving this breakthrough we attribute our success to leveraging the unique capabilities of both tensor networks and quantum circuits.

Therefore, computer-assisted cancer care relies heavily on histopathology images to provide valuable insights. As a result, there is a growing need for precise cell nucleus segmentation within these images. To achieve this, a novel attention-based U-Net framework is presented, incorporating both global and local attention mechanisms to enhance segmentation performance. A key point process model that depends on the past occurrences is the nonlinear Hawkes process, which is used to model relationships, both excitatory and inhibitory, between events of different types. We have investigated a nonlinear Hawkes process with a specific parameter structure that facilitates estimation via generalized method of moments, also exploring its asymptotic properties. Moreover, we have derived closed-form expressions for the expected values that are necessary for the calculations, developing a formula for the expected values of a specific parameter structure, which we call the 'graphical moment'. We have further demonstrated that this approach yields consistent estimates when a particular condition is met: the sum of the strengths of the connections between events of different types is finite. We have also established the asymptotic normality of the estimates under certain conditions, which holds true whether the point processes are stationary or not. We have implemented our methods in an R package called nmfR, which provides tools for fitting the model and generating synthetic data.

Semi-Supervised Learning (SSL) techniques are being developed to combine a small set of annotated images with a larger, unlabeled dataset in order to circumvent this issue. One such method involves leveraging normal data to train an unbiased density model, which then enables the construction of a more balanced Convolutional Neural Network. Furthermore, a new loss function is designed to correct for labeling disparities, which is used in combination with the adversarial loss to train two joint processes. A straightforward examination indicates that this 1.5 order formalism is inherently defective in all contexts. Although it appears that the associated algebra is closed, a detailed examination in a simplified setting reveals the presence of a non-nilpotent BRS operator generated by the 1.5 order formalism. limitations of traditional solid-state optics due to their restricted damage thresholds pose significant challenges, making the investigation of plasma-based components more compelling. We're exploring the potential of using plasma-based components, particularly those based on hydrogen-like ions, as mirrors for high-power laser pulses. These components could provide higher damage thresholds, essential for effectively utilizing the intensity of such lasers. Using a quantum mechanical model, we simulated the interaction between a negatively charged electron and a positively charged ion in the presence of a polarized electromagnetic wave, represented by a recent experimental study. We determined the ion's charge distribution and its interaction with the laser field, which is critical for preventing laser light from passing through. By comparing our detailed quantum mechanical model with a simpler classical approach, we found that the ion's charge distribution plays a crucial role in preventing laser light from passing through, meeting the requirements set by experimental data. We also established that our detailed quantum mechanical description is more accurate than a classical model, which only considers the ion's charge distribution without accounting for its precise spatial arrangement.

Delensing, the process to extract a buried primordial signal from a distorted lens, is crucial for achieving this goal. It involves removing the effect of gravitational lensing induced by weak gravitational fields, primarily caused by massive galactic halos. For this purpose, a machine learning algorithm called Neural Density Estimation (NDE) can be an effective tool in delensing images of the CMB. Initially, NDE trains on a limited set of noisy observations to model the underlying primordial signal, and subsequently uses this model to remove the lensing effect. Furthermore, it is observed that NDE delensing preserves the statistical correlations between pixels, resulting in more accurate results when compared to other methods like mean-removal. Nevertheless, a major limitation of this algorithm is the extensive computational requirement to run it on large images of the CMB. Nevertheless, a variant of NDE called Neural Density Forest (NDF) is proposed, where instead of a global model, a collection of simpler models are trained on a range of mass maps, allowing for faster delensing of the CMB. It is found that NDF delensing demonstrates similar accuracy as NDE, representing a promising advancement for future CMB experiments.

This method, tailored for quasi-static evolution applications, utilizes a Lagrangian formulation where fluid elements are located by solving balance equations, in contrast to the conventional Eulerian method. This innovative approach eschews the use of the Euler equation's first integral, often obtained through adiabatic approximation assumptions, instead directly addressing the complications arising from cooling and gravitational waves. However, electromagnetic analysis of gravitational waves necessitates the rapid identification of signals from gravitational waves in real-time.
